changes.before: Double each own enumerable string-keyed finite numeric property into a new object. Preserve the source; exclude inherited properties. Empty input returns an empty object.
changes.after: Turn an object's values into pairs, change them, and build a new object.

before: Object.entries(object) returns an array of [key,value] pairs for own enumerable string-keyed properties. Inherited properties and symbol keys are excluded. Here the input is a plain data object with finite numeric own values; no getters or hostile proxies are part of the contract.

Object.fromEntries(pairs) takes an iterable of key/value pairs and returns a new ordinary object. Repeated keys keep the last supplied value. This builds an object; it does not modify the source or install a sanitization policy. The loop’s [key,value] syntax destructures each pair; pairs.push(pair) appends one pair and returns the array’s new length, which we ignore.
Implement doubleOwn by transforming entries, not by iterating inherited names. Optional practice: call Object.fromEntries([["read",1],["read",5]]) and explain why the resulting own read value is 5.
after:
`Object.entries(source)` gives an array of `[key, value]` pairs.

It includes own properties: ones stored directly on the object. They must have text keys and be enumerable, meaning marked to appear when listing properties this way. It leaves out inherited properties and symbol keys.

This exercise uses ordinary stored numbers, not properties that run code when read.

`Object.fromEntries(pairs)` builds a new object from key-value pairs. If a key appears twice, the later value wins.

In the loop, `[key, value]` gives a name to each part of a pair. `pairs.push(...)` adds a new pair to the end of the array.

Complete `doubleOwn(source)`. Read its entries, double each number, and build a new object from the changed pairs.

Keep the source unchanged. Empty input should return a new empty object. The supplied values are finite numbers.

before: Make one change to the starter.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
after: Make a new pair with each key and twice its value.
Check that inherited values are left out and the source is unchanged.

before.question: If Object.fromEntries receives [["x", 2], ["x", 7]], what is the final x value?
before.explanation: Both pairs define the same own key; the later supplied value replaces the earlier one.

after.question: If Object.fromEntries receives [["x", 2], ["x", 7]], what is the final x value?
after.explanation: The later pair uses the same key, so its value 7 replaces 2.
